lead: This unit gives the base vocabulary for microprocessors and microcontrollers: what a processor is, how a computer is organized, how programs live in memory, and why designs differ. After it you can read a block diagram, compare von Neumann and Harvard machines, explain CISC and RISC choices, size a memory map, and estimate pipeline speedup.
about: Chapter 1.1 traces microprocessor evolution and separates a microprocessor from a microcontroller. Chapter 1.2 builds the block diagram of a computer: CPU, memory, buses and input/output, with data and control paths. Chapter 1.3 explains the stored-program idea, the fetch-decode-execute cycle, instruction format basics, and the von Neumann versus Harvard split. Chapter 1.4 turns to CISC and RISC design philosophy. Chapter 1.5 covers memory types, the memory hierarchy, address space and memory organization. Chapter 1.6 introduces pipelining: stages, throughput, speedup and hazards. Each chapter uses small numbers so the ideas can be checked by hand. Detailed 8085, 8086 and 8051 designs come in later units.

chapters.idea: A microprocessor is a CPU on a chip; a microcontroller adds memory, timers and I/O on the same chip, and both evolved by shrinking transistors and increasing bit width.
chapters.depth: Cover generations from 4-bit to 64-bit and SoC in one timeline. Define microprocessor, microcontroller, CPU, MPU, MCU and embedded system. Compare on chip count, cost, power, RAM/ROM, I/O, timers and use. Some syllabi call the comparison microprocessor vs microcontroller. Keep 8085 and 8051 as named examples only; do not draw their pin diagrams.

figure.aria: A tree splits processors into microprocessors, which need external memory and I/O, and microcontrollers, which include ROM, RAM, timers and I/O ports on one chip.

chapters.example: An 8051-based washing-machine board has a CPU, 4 KB program ROM, 128 B RAM, two timers and 32 I/O pins on one chip. A desktop board uses an 8086 CPU with separate RAM, ROM, timer and I/O chips. Classify each as microprocessor or microcontroller and give two reasons.
chapters.trap: Calling every small CPU a microcontroller; a microcontroller must include on-chip memory and peripherals. Also, bit width is not the same as addressable memory size.
chapters.prereq: None; assumes the basic idea of a computer.
chapters.leave: Detailed 8085 and 8051 architecture, pins and SFRs to Unit 2 and Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A computer moves data and instructions between CPU, memory and I/O over three buses, with the CPU controlling the sequence.
chapters.depth: Draw the general-purpose processor block: ALU, registers, control unit, program counter, instruction register and flags. Explain address bus, data bus, control bus; bus width and address space; read/write control; memory-mapped I/O vs isolated I/O at concept level; I/O ports and simple polling or interrupt idea. Introduce data path and control path. Mention generic read/write bus timing: address valid, read strobe, data sampled; leave 8085 machine cycles to Unit 2. Some syllabi call this computer organization or block diagram of a general purpose processor.

figure.aria: A CPU connects through a bus system carrying address, data and control signals to memory and to input and output devices.

chapters.example: A simple computer has 16 address lines and 8 data lines. Find its address space in bytes and the largest byte it can transfer in one bus cycle. It uses an 8 KB ROM and a 2 KB RAM; how many address lines does each need?
chapters.trap: Confusing address bus width with data bus width; 16 address lines give 64 KB, not 16 KB. Also, memory-mapped I/O uses memory instructions, isolated I/O uses special IN/OUT.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1 for processor terms; basic binary powers.
chapters.leave: 8085/8086 pin signals, timing diagrams and machine cycles to Unit 2; 8255/8253/8259 interfacing to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: The stored-program concept keeps instructions and data in the same memory, so the CPU repeatedly fetches, decodes and executes; Harvard machines separate program and data memories.
chapters.depth: Explain stored program, program counter, instruction register, fetch-decode-execute cycle, instruction format: opcode and operands; encoding of a simple instruction; addressing concept: immediate, direct, indirect, register and register indirect at intro level. Compare von Neumann (shared memory, one bus) and Harvard (separate program/data memories and buses, can fetch instruction and data together). Use 8086 as von Neumann and 8051 as Harvard example, but no detailed architecture. Some syllabi call this Von-Neumann Vs Harvard architecture.

figure.aria: Two CPUs are shown: one connects to a shared memory holding code and data, and the other connects separately to program memory and data memory.

chapters.example: An 8051 has 4 KB program memory and 128 B data memory. A von Neumann CPU has one 64 KB memory for code and data. For each, state whether the same address can hold an instruction byte and a data byte, and give one advantage of its design.
chapters.trap: Saying Harvard always has two separate external chips; the split can be internal. Also, stored-program does not mean code and data always share one physical memory—Harvard keeps them separate.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2 for CPU, memory and buses.
chapters.leave: Detailed instruction formats, addressing modes and assembly to Unit 3; 8085 timing to Unit 2; 8051 memory map and SFRs to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: CISC spends hardware on complex instructions to reduce program size; RISC keeps instructions simple and regular so pipelining and compilers work well.
chapters.depth: Define CISC and RISC. Compare instruction length (variable vs fixed), number of addressing modes, register set, load-store vs memory operands, microcode vs hardwired control, CPI and code size, compiler role, pipeline friendliness. Use 8086 as CISC and ARM as RISC; mention 8051 as CISC-like but do not list its instruction set. Some syllabi call these complex instruction set computer and reduced instruction set computer. Keep the debate practical: no design is always faster.

figure.aria: A tree divides instruction set design into CISC, with variable length and many addressing modes, and RISC, with fixed length load-store instructions suited to pipelining.

chapters.example: A CISC CPU has 120 instructions and averages 4 clock cycles per instruction. A RISC CPU has 40 instructions and averages 1.2 clock cycles per instruction. A program needs 10^6 CISC instructions and 1.4 × 10^6 RISC instructions. Find clock cycles for each and the RISC/CISC time ratio at the same clock frequency.
chapters.trap: Assuming RISC always executes fewer instructions or always wins; RISC often needs more instructions. Compare total cycles = instruction count × CPI, not CPI alone.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3 for instruction format and fetch cycle.
chapters.leave: 8051 instruction set classification and addressing modes to Unit 3 and Unit 4; ARM instruction set and CPSR to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Memory is a hierarchy chosen by speed, size and cost, and memory organization maps address lines to chips and locations.
chapters.depth: Define bit, byte, word, address, capacity, volatile/non-volatile. Cover RAM (SRAM, DRAM), ROM (mask, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, flash), cache, main memory, secondary storage; memory hierarchy. Explain address space = 2^n for n address lines; byte-addressable vs word-addressable; address decoding; chip select; memory map; read-only vs read-write regions; stack concept at overview. Use a 16-bit address example. Mention 8051 separate program/data spaces only as an example; leave SFRs and external memory connection to Unit 4.

figure.aria: A memory hierarchy stack runs from registers at the top through cache, main memory and flash to hard disk or tape at the bottom, getting slower and larger.

chapters.example: A byte-addressable memory has 16 address lines. An 8 KB ROM is placed at 0000H and a 2 KB RAM at 2000H. Find the address range of the ROM and the RAM, and the total address space.
chapters.trap: End address is start + size − 1, not start + size. Also, 8 KB is 8192 bytes, not 8000 bytes; 1 K = 1024.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2 for address bus and buses; basic powers of 2.
chapters.leave: 8085 memory interfacing and address decoding to Unit 2; 8051 memory organization and SFRs to Unit 4; cache replacement policies to advanced computer architecture.

chapters.idea: Pipelining overlaps stages of different instructions so throughput rises, but one instruction's latency and hazards limit the gain.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach pipelining this early; keep it to basics. Define pipeline, stage, throughput, latency, CPI, clock cycle and speedup. Draw a 5-stage IF-ID-EX-MEM-WB pipeline. Compute time with and without pipeline: k + n − 1 cycles vs nk cycles. Explain fill/drain, ideal speedup k, hazards: structural, data and control; one-line fixes: stall, forwarding, branch prediction. Link to RISC. No superscalar details.

figure.aria: A five-stage pipeline timeline for four instructions shows each instruction starting one cycle after the previous one, with stages IF, ID, EX, MEM and WB overlapping.

chapters.example: A 5-stage pipeline runs 4 independent instructions. Each stage takes one clock cycle of 2 ns. Find total time without pipelining, total time with pipelining, and the speedup.
chapters.trap: Using nk cycles for a pipeline; the correct count is k + n − 1 for n independent instructions. Also, pipeline speedup is limited by the slowest stage and hazards, and cannot exceed k.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3 and 4 for instruction cycle and RISC design.
chapters.leave: Detailed hazard handling, superscalar and ARM pipeline to Unit 6; 8085/8086 timing to Unit 2.

links: processor terms feed into computer block diagram
buses carry the fetch from memory
instruction format shapes CISC and RISC
program and data placement uses memory organization
address bus width fixes memory size
memory access time sets pipeline stage balance
chip evolution explains the CISC to RISC shift
